title: Git Fundamentals
description: Basic commands and concepts in Git

content.overview: In this module, you'll learn the fundamental Git commands and concepts that form the basis of version control with Git. You'll understand the Git workflow, including the working directory, staging area, and repository.

steps.title: Git Workflow Overview
steps.content: Git has three main areas: the working directory (where you edit files), the staging area (where you prepare changes for a commit), and the repository (where Git stores the history of your project). Understanding this workflow is essential for using Git effectively.

steps.title: Checking Status
steps.content: The `git status` command shows the state of your working directory and staging area. It lets you see which changes have been staged, which haven't, and which files aren't being tracked by Git.

commands.description: Check the status of your working directory
commands.expectedOutput:
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	hello.txt

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

behindTheCommand.title: How Git Tracks File Status
behindTheCommand.content:
When you run `git status`, Git compares the files in your working directory, staging area, and the most recent commit. It categorizes files as:

- Untracked: New files that Git doesn't yet track
- Modified: Tracked files with changes not yet staged
- Staged: Files ready to be committed
- Unmodified: Tracked files with no changes since the last commit

Git uses the index file in the .git directory to keep track of the staging area state.

steps.title: Adding Files
steps.content: The `git add` command adds changes in your working directory to the staging area. It tells Git that you want to include updates to a particular file in the next commit.

commands.description: Add the file to the staging area

commands.expectedOutput:
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   hello.txt

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens During git add
behindTheCommand.content: When you run `git add`, Git calculates a checksum for each file (using the SHA-1 hash algorithm), stores that version of the file in the Git repository (as a blob), and adds that checksum to the staging area. When you run `git commit`, Git checksums each subdirectory and stores them as a tree object in the Git repository. Then Git creates a commit object that has the metadata and a pointer to the root project tree so it can re-create that snapshot when needed.

steps.title: Committing Changes
steps.content: The `git commit` command saves your staged changes to the repository. A commit is like a snapshot of your project at a specific point in time.

commands.description: Commit the staged changes with a message
commands.expectedOutput:
[master (root-commit) xxxxxxx] Add hello.txt file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 hello.txt

On branch master
nothing to commit, working tree clean

behindTheCommand.title: Anatomy of a Commit
behindTheCommand.content:
A Git commit contains:

- A commit hash (SHA-1 identifier)
- Author information (name and email)
- Timestamp (date and time)
- Commit message
- Reference to the tree object representing the project state
- References to parent commit(s)

Each commit (except the first one) points to its parent commit(s), forming a directed acyclic graph of your project's history.

steps.title: Viewing History
steps.content: The `git log` command shows the commit history of your repository. It allows you to see the commit messages, authors, dates, and commit hashes.

commands.expectedOutput:
commit xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx (HEAD -> master)
Author: Your Name <your.email@example.com>
Date:   Wed Jan 1 12:00:00 2025 -0500

    Add hello.txt file

behindTheCommand.title: Traversing the Commit Graph
behindTheCommand.content:
When you run `git log`, Git starts at the current HEAD and traverses the commit graph by following each commit's pointer to its parent(s). This creates a linear history view, even though the underlying structure might be a complex directed acyclic graph (especially with branches and merges).

Git uses the references in the .git/refs directory to know where branches point in the commit graph.

steps.title: Making Changes
steps.content: Let's modify our file and see how Git tracks changes to existing files.

commands.description: Add another line to the file

commands.expectedOutput:
On branch master
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   hello.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

diff --git a/hello.txt b/hello.txt
index xxxxxxx..xxxxxxx 100644
--- a/hello.txt
+++ b/hello.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Hello, Git!
+Another line.

behindTheCommand.title: How Git Tracks Changes
behindTheCommand.content:
Git doesn't store file differences; instead, it stores complete snapshots of your files at each commit. For efficiency, if a file hasn't changed, Git stores a reference to the previous identical file it has already stored.

When you run `git diff`, Git compares the working directory with the staging area. It shows lines that were added with a '+' prefix and removed lines with a '-' prefix.

steps.title: Staging and Committing Changes
steps.content: Now let's stage and commit our changes to the repository.

commands.expectedOutput:
On branch master
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	modified:   hello.txt

commands.command: git commit -m "Add another line to hello.txt"
commands.expectedOutput:
[master xxxxxxx] Add another line to hello.txt
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

xxxxxxx (HEAD -> master) Add another line to hello.txt
xxxxxxx Add hello.txt file

steps.title: Viewing Changes Between Commits
steps.content: You can use `git diff` with commit references to see changes between different commits.

commands.description: Compare the previous commit with the current one
commands.expectedOutput:
diff --git a/hello.txt b/hello.txt
index xxxxxxx..xxxxxxx 100644
--- a/hello.txt
+++ b/hello.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Hello, Git!
+Another line.

behindTheCommand.title: Commit References in Git
behindTheCommand.content:
Git provides several ways to refer to commits:

- Full SHA-1 hash: `git show a1b2c3d4e5f6...`
- Abbreviated hash: `git show a1b2c3d`
- HEAD: The current commit your working directory is based on
- HEAD~1: The commit before HEAD
- HEAD~2: Two commits before HEAD
- Branch names: `git show master`
- Tags: `git show v1.0`

These references make it easier to navigate the commit history without memorizing commit hashes.
